content_voiceover: This page has three linked questions on inhibitor management strategy. The first asks about appropriate treatment for an acute knee bleed in a hemophilia A patient with an inhibitor. If the inhibitor is low responding, factor eight concentrate itself can still work as first line therapy. If it's high responding, you switch to bypassing agents, recombinant factor seven a or activated prothrombin complex concentrate. If the patient is already on non-factor prophylaxis like emicizumab, the appropriate acute treatment is still a bypassing agent, preferentially factor eight if the inhibitor allows or a bypassing agent otherwise, with caution around aPCC dosing because of thrombotic risk when combined with emicizumab, not aPCC used indiscriminately as first choice, and simply raising the emicizumab dose is not an appropriate way to treat acute bleeding since emicizumab isn't titrated like a rescue drug. The second question is a one and a half year old with severe hemophilia A and a high titer inhibitor of fourteen point eight Bethesda units, and asks which management step is wrong. Everything about using bypassing agents for acute bleeds, weekly subcutaneous emicizumab prophylaxis to reduce bleed frequency, and using anti-CD20 or immunosuppression if the inhibitor persists despite ITI, are all correct. The error is using plasma derived factor eight to treat an acute bleed in a high inhibitor patient, since the inhibitor will simply neutralize it, making it an inappropriate acute treatment choice. The third question, contrasting hemophilia A and B broadly, tests background facts, hemophilia A is far more common than B, severe disease is defined as factor activity under one percent, both are X-linked recessive, and long term prophylaxis prevents joint bleeding and preserves quality of life and joint health, but the false statement is that twenty five to thirty five percent of hemophilia B patients develop inhibitors, that rate is actually much lower than in hemophilia A, closer to three to five percent.
keypoints: Low-responding inhibitors may still respond to factor VIII; high-responding inhibitors need bypassing agents
On emicizumab prophylaxis, breakthrough bleeds still need a bypassing agent, not a higher emicizumab dose
Plasma-derived factor VIII will be neutralized in a high-titer inhibitor patient, so it's the wrong acute treatment
Hemophilia A is more common than B; both are X-linked recessive with severe defined as under 1% activity
Inhibitor rates are much lower in hemophilia B (roughly 3-5%) than the 25-35% seen in hemophilia A
keypoint_voiceover: Three exam traps to remember. Low responding inhibitors can still be treated with factor eight, but high responding inhibitors need a bypassing agent, and being on emicizumab prophylaxis does not change that, you still bypass for acute bleeds rather than pushing the emicizumab dose higher. Giving plasma derived factor eight to a patient with a high titer inhibitor is a mistake because the inhibitor neutralizes it. And don't confuse the inhibitor rates between the two hemophilias, hemophilia B has a much lower inhibitor rate, around three to five percent, compared to hemophilia A.
